terms.comment: To two or more people: Quid agitis?, Ut valētis? (Traupman 17).

terms.grammar: question: quī, the old ablative “how?”, with valēre, be well
evidence: Traupman 17: how are you?, quī valēs?
terms.comment: Lewis & Short has quī “how?” in questions as classical; this question with valēs is Traupman’s.

terms.latin: Quō pactō rēs sē tibi habent?
terms.grammar: question: “in what way do things hold themselves for you?”
evidence: Traupman 18: how are things with you?, quō pactō rēs sē tibi habent?
terms.comment: Traupman’s phrase, made of classical parts (quō pactō, how; rēs sē habent, things stand); Lewis & Short does not quote it whole. Comedy asks Quid agitur? (Ter. Ad. 883).

phrases.latin: Salvē, Baba! Ut valēs? — Bene, mī Theodōre.
phrases.english: Hello, Baba! How are you? — Fine, my Theo.

sources: Lewis & Short: valeo
